Mathematicians use different number sets for different purposes. Distinguishing them is
not a vocabulary game: the classification tells you which operations are always possible
and which values count as solutions.

Place value and the role of zero
Our number system is called base ten because each position is worth ten times the
position to its right. The digit 4 can stand for 4 ones, 4 tens, 4 hundreds or 4 tenths; the
The highlighted 8 means 8 ones, not 8 thousands.
Place-value columns for 3,048.307. The decimal point marks the boundary between whole-number places and fractional places.
Figure 1.2 Each place is ten times the one on its right. A decimal point separates whole-number positions from positions
representing tenths, hundredths and smaller parts.
Moving one place to the left multiplies the value of a digit by 10. Moving one place to the right
divides it by 10. This is why multiplying a number by 10 does not require inventing new digits:
every digit shifts one place left. A zero appears at the end of a whole number because there are no
units in that position, not because zero is being “added”.
Zero has two related jobs. As a number, it marks a position on the number line between the positive
and negative integers. As a digit, it holds an empty place so that the other digits keep their intended
values. Without the zero in 3,048, the digits would read 348 and mean a completely different
quantity. Without the zero in 3.05, the digit 5 would shift into the tenths place and produce 3.5.

Data are not just numbers. A data set records a characteristic of each individual, and the
type of that characteristic decides which table, graph and average are appropriate.
Classifying the data correctly is the first step in any honest analysis.
A data set is a collection of observations. Each person or object described is an individual; each
characteristic recorded is a variable. In a survey of 30 students, the individuals are the students
and the variables might be year group, favourite fruit and journey time. A single row of a table
describes one individual; a single column describes one variable.
Variables fall into two broad families. Categorical data place individuals in groups. Numerical data
record a quantity. Categorical data may be nominal, with no natural order, such as transport mode,
or ordinal, with a meaningful order, such as a satisfaction rating from “very dissatisfied” to “very
satisfied”. Numerical data may be discrete, taking separate countable values such as the number of
siblings, or continuous, taking any value in a range such as height or journey time.
Any value in a range, limited only by the measuring
The classification is about the variable, not the way it is written. A rating of 1 to 5 is often treated as
ordinal categorical data because the numbers label ordered categories. A journey time recorded as
“15 minutes” is still continuous data, even though the response has been rounded to a whole
number. What matters is what the values represent.
